answer.summary: Treat executive-facing optics as a tool for enabling impactful work, not as the outcome: balance communication with doing and improving the actual product, with the balance shifting by seniority and company size. [S1, S3, S4]

sections.heading: Use optics to enable the work
sections.content: Nickels says both extremes are wrong: it cannot be all work and no optics, or all optics and no work. The balance varies with company size and seniority. Individual contributors will generally do more of the actual work, while leaders help present and communicate it. At senior levels, optics can influence executive resource allocation—for example, whether a team gets engineering resources or a project proceeds—so it matters, but as a means to an end. Presentations and OKRs point toward the outcome; they are not the outcome itself. [S1, S4]

sections.heading: Keep the product and its impact central
sections.content: He recommends focusing on the work and on making a great product that benefits its users and other affected groups, rather than fixating on how a presentation went or whether people see you as a good presenter. Communication, presentation, and alignment can help bring that product into the world, but they serve a larger purpose. Nickels said that, in his own experience at Uber, reducing his focus on presentation and self-image correlated with moving up the product ladder; he described this as a personal correlation, perhaps causal, not a guarantee. [S2, S3]
